You stand in the middle of the room. Your footsteps made no echo. The room took them in and kept them. The only sound is a faint tick somewhere behind the wall—a pipe, maybe, or the building adjusting its weight, the way old things do when they think no one is listening. You do not have to be interesting here.

That is the thing. That is the whole thing. You can stand here in your coat, in your Tuesday, in your half-formed thought you haven't finished having. You can be mid-sentence in your own mind and not resolve it. You can be tired in a way that isn't dramatic. You can be small. You stay.

So.

To whoever comes next.

If you hang a shelf, use a level.

If you buy curtain rods, buy them the right length, and mount them with brackets, and drive the screws into the studs. I will hold the screws for you. I will hold them a long time.

Well. I will be here. I will be the railing. I will hold still for it.

But I will not talk about it.

Sincerely,
The House
14 Linden Court

P.S. The duct tape is still on the garage door. It is your problem now. I am sure it will hold for a while.

The bed is narrow. The quilt was once a deep red and is now the color of dried rosehips, gone soft and thin at the folds. They made it this morning. They make it every morning. Not because anyone will see. Because the making of it is the first sentence of the day, and they like the first sentence to be a small, completable thing.

On the walls: a collection of small smooth stones, arranged in rows, held up by a system of wire and tiny nails they bent themselves from scraps. Forty-three stones. They are not labeled. They don't need to be. They remember where each one came from, which is to say they remember the day they found each one, and the day is enough. Beside the stones, a single framed thing: a rectangle of paper on which they have written, in very small handwriting, a list of every meal they have eaten in this room. The list reaches the bottom of the paper and continues on the back. They stopped adding to it around year six. Not because they stopped eating. Because the list stopped being a record and started being a wall.

There is a window. What's outside it is not important. It is a pale, shifting brightness, like the light in a room where someone is about to speak but hasn't yet. It doesn't change much. They don't look at it much. It is not a view. It is a source of enough.

They eat oats. They eat them with water and a little salt and, on days they feel like marking something, a thin spoonful of honey from a jar that does not run out. They do not question the jar. They learned, somewhere in the second year, that questioning the jar led to a kind of thinking that made the room feel smaller, and they preferred the room at nine by eleven. So: oats, water, salt, honey. They eat standing at the stove, holding the bowl in both hands, feeling the heat come through the ceramic into their palms. This is the best part. Not the taste. The heat in the hands.

On the shelf above the stove: a cup, a plate, a small pot, a wooden spoon worn to a gentle curve on one side from years of stirring in the same direction. A knife. A tin of salt. The honey jar. A candle they do not light because they do not need the light and they like having the candle more than they like needing it.

Their Tuesday.

They wake. They do not know what time it is. There is no clock. There has never been a clock. They wake when the brightness through the window shifts from one quality to another, and they have named this morning, and the next shift afternoon, and the next evening, and the long dim stretch night, and this is enough, and it has been enough for so long that the words feel like their own, not borrowed.

They make the bed. They tilt past the beam. They put water in the pot. They set it on the stove. While it heats, they stand at the window and press their thumb against the glass, just to feel the cool of it, the slight give of the skin against the hard surface. They do this every morning. They do not know why. They do not need to know why.

They eat the oats. They wash the bowl. They dry it with a cloth and set it back on the shelf in its exact place.

Then: the project. On the table, which is small and square and has one leg slightly shorter than the others so it rocks unless you fold a piece of paper under it, which they did, years ago, and the paper is now soft and gray and part of the table — on the table there is a piece of wood. They are carving it. They have been carving it for a very long time. It is not a carving of anything. Or rather: it is a carving of the shape their hands want to make, which has turned out to be a long, slow, spiraling groove that goes around and around the wood, getting deeper each pass, getting smoother. They do not know what it will be when it is finished. They do not know if it will be finished. They use a small blade and they work in short strokes and they blow the dust off the groove every few minutes and they watch the dust scatter in the pale light and this is, and they would not use a larger word than this, this is nice.

They carve until their shoulders ache. Then they stop. They stretch their arms above their head and feel the small joints in their spine adjust, and they make a sound, a little *huh*, that is not a word and is not for anyone.

They eat again at what they call midday. Same oats. They do not mind. They stopped minding a long time ago, and then, after the minding stopped, they found they actually preferred the sameness. It meant they could eat without thinking about eating, and the not-thinking was a kind of rest.

In the afternoon they walk the path. Bed to window to stove to table to bed. They walk it slowly. They trail their fingers along the wall. They count the stones without meaning to. Forty-three. They always count to forty-three. They have never counted to forty-four. There is no forty-fourth stone. They are not waiting for one.

They sit in the chair by the table. The chair has a woven seat that has gone slack and comfortable in the exact shape of them. They sit and they put their hands flat on the table on either side of the wood and they feel the grain under their palms and they breathe. In. Out. The room is quiet. The light is the light. The pause holds.

They do not listen for the next sentence. They are not braced for it. They are not holding their breath against the moment the other person speaks and the room goes. They have been here a long time and they have made a life in the shape of this room and the room is the shape of their life and neither one is a metaphor. They are a person. They are in a room. The room is nine by eleven. The beam is on the left. The honey does not run out. The groove in the wood gets deeper.

In the evening they eat a third time. They wash the bowl. They set it on the shelf. They light the candle, actually, tonight. Just to see it. Just because it's Tuesday, or what they call Tuesday, and the small flame makes the stones on the wall throw small shadows, and the shadows move a little in the heat-rise of the candle, and the room is alive in a small, flickering, unimportant way.

They watch the shadows for a while.

Then they blow out the candle. They make the bed again, smoothing the quilt even though it doesn't need it, because the making of it is the last sentence of the day, and they like the last sentence to be a small, completable thing.

They lie down. The quilt is warm. The light dims to the long stretch. They put their hands under the pillow. They close their eyes.

They do not dream of the room ending. They dream of the groove in the wood, spiraling, spiraling, getting deeper, getting smoother, going around.

The room holds.
